Endoplasmic Reticulum (ER)
System of membranous tubes and sacs known as cisternae
intracellular highway’ 
a path that molecules travel to move from one part of the cell to another
Quantity of ER  in a cell varies depending on its activity level
Two types:
Rough
Smooth
Continuous–form an interconnected network
explanation: The Endoplasmic Reticulum (ER) is a system of membranous tubes and sacs called cisternae. It functions as an 'intracellular highway', providing a pathway for molecules to travel from one part of the cell to another. The total amount of ER in a cell varies based on its activity level. The ER is divided into two continuous types that form an interconnected network: Rough ER and Smooth ER.

questions.q: What are the membranous tubes and sacs of the Endoplasmic Reticulum called?
questions.exp: The slide defines the ER as a system of membranous tubes and sacs known as cisternae.

questions.q: Why is the Endoplasmic Reticulum nicknamed the 'intracellular highway'?
opts: It exports waste directly outside the cell.
It is a path that molecules travel to move from one part of the cell to another.
It is the site of cell division.
It connects different cells in a colonial organism.
questions.exp: The ER is called the 'intracellular highway' because it is a path that molecules travel to move from one part of the cell to another.
